paras: The expulsion of Walter Bryant from Reading, Ohio, took place on the night of August 23, 1900, when a crowd of about forty seized Bryant, a Black youth, put a noose around his neck, tied him to a tree and drove him out of town. Bryant was released at the town limits with a warning that he would be lynched if he came back. The story, credited to the New York World, was reprinted in North Carolina under a headline stressing that the violence took place in Ohio.

According to the report, Bryant was a "negro boy" who had "drifted into" Reading, described as a "rockbound democratic suburb," a few days earlier. The same account stated that "Reading citizens do not allow negroes in their town"; it reported no accusation against him.

At about 8 o'clock on Thursday evening, Bryant saw a crowd at his door and heard cries of "Hang him!" and "String him up!" Several men rushed in, slipped his head into a noose and dragged him outside. He broke away and hid in an apple barrel, but was caught again and tied to a tree, where, the report said, he cried, prayed and begged to be spared.
The crowd then escorted him to the town limits and warned him never to show his face in Reading again. No injuries were reported, and the account closed by saying he "ran down the road like a deer."
No report of arrests, an official inquiry or any response from Reading authorities appears in the coverage.

The episode is known only from a New York World story that the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger reprinted on August 31 under the headline "This in Ohio" and the deck "Negro Boy Driven Out of Town Because He Is a Negro." By heading the story "This in Ohio," the Messenger presented it as news of racial violence in the North. The World text called the night "the most violent scare of his life" and dwelt on Bryant's fear without naming anyone in the crowd.
No account of the episode was found in Ohio papers or in the Black press.
